Ana Giraldo-Wingler — Portfolio

Design, code, and writing have been my primary creative mediums since 2001. A recent immigrant with no friends, I coded forums from scratch in PHP, HTML, and CSS with the Acer Inspire desktop running Windows XP in my parents' New Jersey basement. I tweaked vector art, maintained a blog, made tutorials about how to use 3D Studio Max, and animated Hello Kitty-inspired gifs.

Grown-up me is a product person, engineer, and writer with twelve years moving between brand, prototype, production, and poems. Among other things I've built an algorithmic poetry generator The Observer wrote about and Walmart's first production LLM application.

VICE & AL JAZEERA · 2012–2014 · VIDEO JOURNALISM

Documentary work, before any of this

—

Where the storytelling instinct actually started.

My first job out of college was in video journalism. At VICE, I produced a documentary about beauty and aesthetics in Medellín, Colombia, in the wake of narcoterrorism — it passed a million views on YouTube. At Al Jazeera, I was a production assistant on the Fault Lines documentary "Life After Guantanamo," about detainees adjusting to release after 11, 12, 13 years of unjust detention.

Everything I've built since, the products, the writing, the case studies on this page, comes out of the same instinct that sent me to Medellín and to that story: find the people actually living a thing, and tell it straight.

GIRLFRIENDS LABS · 2015–2018 · PYTHON · NLTK · WIKIPEDIA API

Wikisonnet (& experiments in generative text)

—

An algorithmic poetry generator that turned any topic into a sonnet.

I shaped the parameters and built the frontend. A colleague built the actual generation engine in Python's NLTK, pulling source material from the Wikipedia API and assembling it into the correct meter and rhyme scheme. It was an early experiment in generative text.

The Observer wrote about the project and my team presented the process behind it at xCoAx and Internet Yama-Ichi.

The constraints were the more interesting part of this project: teaching a system the parameters of a sonnet and watching what it did with them. Some of the poems were eloquent and moving in a way, despite being something I don't think a human mind would write.

In Other Words (Playgiarize)

—

A synonym engine to process poems I loved.

The app took text as an input and would replace words with synonyms pulled from the Dictionary.com API. I ran it on "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" and some of my other favorite poems. I was curious about what stays meaningful in a piece of writing when the author's specific choices are changed.

PROCESSING FOUNDATION · 2017–2018 · UX RESEARCH · COMMUNITY · EDUCATION

p5.js Web Editor

—

Product and design work for the browser-based version of Processing.

A lot of people, many of them students, use p5.js to learn to code by creating art, animation, and interactive sketches. I worked as PM and designer on its web editor through the Processing Foundation, interviewing the teachers building lesson plans around it and watching students use it in real classrooms.

I also built and ran the continuous feedback loop with the wider community, an audience that ranged from total beginners to working artists, in order to capture qualitative feedback in a broad way. My goal was to ensure the tool was welcoming for people who'd never written code before while keeping it robust for power users.

WALMART · 2023–2024 · LLM · RAG · PRODUCT NAMING

Symphony, Ensemble & Sage

—

Three early GenAI concepts for Walmart's different audiences.

Walmart's Chief Product Officer challenged our team to find where AI could create real impact in 2023, not in some hand-wavy future. Dozens of interviews across store associates, corporate teams, and customers surfaced three pain points, each getting its own product: Symphony, an AI scheduling tool for store managers; Ensemble, a knowledge-base dashboard for corporate teams; and Sage, a context-aware concierge for real-time customer support.

I co-led research, design, and prototyping, and named all three products myself. The throughline across them was that the most compelling value people see in AI is for it to give them their time back.

RUSHCUTTERS BAY BOOKS · 2026 — ONGOING · SHOPIFY · STRIPE · TINA / SANITY

Rushcutters Bay Books

—

A publishing imprint's storefront, built by me, currently in progress.

An independent book imprint that publishes forgotten works is launching this fall and needed a site to hold an editable catalog, an author program, and direct-to-reader sales. I'm building it myself, evaluating Tina against Sanity as the CMS layer, and wiring the storefront to Shopify and Stripe for checkout. It's a small build, but it shows that I have my hands on the keyboard ☺︎☺︎☺︎

PERSONAL PROJECT · 2024 — ONGOING · PRIVACY, SYSTEMS, SELF-HOSTING

Personal Digital Archivism

—

Reclaiming and reorganizing 25 years of digital life, on paper and off the cloud.

In 2024 I started going through my own accumulated digital life — old MacBooks, a 240,000-message Gmail archive, iCloud Photos, a decade of half-abandoned accounts on LiveJournal, Xanga, Tumblr, and Geocities, my college application essays, AIM message logs. I'm writing about it as I go, in a running series of essays on my Substack. The rule so far: discover first, preserve second, organize third, delete last. Nothing gets wiped until I actually understand what it is.

Roughly, the digital life in question looks like this. Geocities and AIM in elementary school. Xanga and LiveJournal in middle school. Tumblr and early Gmail through high school and college. Facebook and Twitter through my twenties. iCloud and Google absorbing most of it by my thirties, quietly, without me choosing that.

The practical work has meant YubiKeys for hardware authentication, five months on a flip phone, and a move from Gmail and 1Password to Proton and Bitwarden. The less practical part has meant printing things and working in physical notebooks, because I want to touch the plan sometimes instead of just scrolling it.

The project plan itself, printed out and annotated by hand.
